mainTopic: עירובין 77a: Using the wall between two courtyards. Lifting food onto it, assigning it to the side with easy use, and lowering its height with a removed stone or a buried basin.
overview: This amud deals with the wall between two courtyards. רבי יוחנן says each courtyard may even lift food up onto a narrow wall-top. The גמרא explains that this applies only when the top is smaller than four by four טפחים, and that this fits his ruling reported by רב דימי. רב is stricter, because two courtyards are only rabbinic domains, and חכמים reinforced their own laws. Next, רב נחמן teaches that a wall or a ditch that is easy for one courtyard to use and hard for the other is given to the side with easy use. A צריכותא explains why both cases had to be taught. The גמרא then discusses lowering a wall, either by removing a piece from its top or by placing an overturned basin next to it. This leads to a debate about when a basin buried in the ground may no longer be moved on שבת, and that debate continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן allows lifting food onto the wall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that residents of each courtyard may lift food from their own courtyard onto the wall-top and eat it there.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: These people may lift food up from here and eat, and those people may lift food up from there and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives his ruling on the משנה's case of food on top of the wall. He says each courtyard's residents may even lift food from their courtyard up onto the wall and eat it there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only spoke about climbing up to eat food that was already on the wall. רבי יוחנן goes further and allows moving food from the courtyard up onto the wall. In his view, the wall-top does not block the courtyard from its own food, so carrying up to it is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: they bring up / lift up (an object)
from here (from this side)
they eat

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
phrases.notes: This continues from רב's statement on the previous amud.

phrases.english: These may lift food up from here and eat,
phrases.notes: Residents of the first courtyard.

phrases.english: and those may lift food up from here and eat.
phrases.notes: Residents of the second courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יוחנן's position after רב's statement earlier.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Residents of each courtyard may lift food from their courtyard onto the wall-top and eat it there.

steps.title: The משנה says 'climb,' not 'lift'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן from the משנה's wording, which permits climbing up but implies that lifting food up is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: These may climb up from here and eat, and those may climb up from there and eat. Climbing up is allowed. Lifting food up is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה to attack רבי יוחנן. The משנה says people may 'climb up' (עולין), which implies they may not 'lift up' food (מעלין), and that is exactly what רבי יוחנן allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is built on an inference from exact wording. If lifting food were allowed, the משנה would have said so. By choosing the word 'climb,' it seems to rule out lifting.

keyTerms.meaning: they go up / climb up (themselves)
yes … no (this is allowed, that is not)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two similar words. עוֹלִין means the people themselves climb up. מַעֲלִין means they carry an object up. The whole challenge depends on this difference.

phrases.english: We learned in the Mishnah:
These may climb up from here and eat,
and those may climb up from here and eat.
To climb up, yes; to lift up food, no.
phrases.notes: This is the גמרא's inference, and it contradicts רבי יוחנן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי יוחנן's ruling in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that food may be lifted onto the wall-top.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says only 'climb up,' which implies that lifting food up is forbidden.

steps.title: It depends on the size of the wall-top
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the משנה as covering two cases. On a wall-top of four by four, only climbing is allowed. On a smaller one, lifting food up is allowed too.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the משנה means: if the wall-top is four by four טפחים, climbing up is allowed but lifting food up is not. If it is less than four by four, lifting food up is also allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by explaining what the משנה means (הכי קאמר). It splits the case by the size of the wall-top.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wall-top of four by four טפחים is large enough to count as its own place, so food may not be moved onto it from the courtyard. A smaller wall-top is too small to matter, so lifting food up is fine. רבי יוחנן was talking about that smaller case, so the משנה does not contradict him.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it means (the text is reinterpreted)
four by four (טפחים): the minimum size to count as a significant area
also

phrases.english: This is what it means:
If it has four by four handbreadths,
to climb up, yes; to lift up food, no.
If it does not have four by four handbreadths,
they may lift up food as well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the משנה as describing two cases, split by size
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה forbids lifting food up in every case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban on lifting applies only to a wall-top of four by four. When it is smaller, lifting is allowed, as רבי יוחנן said.
steps.whatToRemember: Size decides the case. Four by four or more: climbing yes, lifting no. Less than four by four: lifting is allowed too.

steps.title: This fits רבי יוחנן's other ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רבי יוחנן is consistent. Through רב דימי he ruled that a small spot between a public and private domain may be used by people from both sides, as long as they don't pass objects between them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן follows his own reasoning. When רב דימי came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a place smaller than four by four טפחים may be used by people of the public domain and people of the private domain to rest their loads on, provided they do not exchange objects.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the answer in step 3 by showing that רבי יוחנן holds the same idea elsewhere. He lets people from two different areas share a small spot, as long as they don't swap items through it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here, too, a spot smaller than four by four is too small to matter, so people from both sides may use it. רבי יוחנן did not worry that they might end up carrying from one domain to the other, except by directly exchanging items. This matches his lenient ruling for the narrow wall-top.

keyTerms.meaning: he follows his own reasoning (he is consistent)
when (he) came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
public domain / private domain
to adjust or rest a load carried on the shoulder
they exchange (pass objects to each other)

steps.whyThisMatters: רב דימי's report of רבי יוחנן (also cited in מסכת שבת 8b) is the basic rule that a small spot under four by four (מקום פטור) may be used by people of both neighboring domains, as long as they don't exchange items through it.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan follows his own reasoning,
for when Rav Dimi came
phrases.notes: From ארץ ישראל to בבל.

phrases.english: he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: מָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה —
phrases.english: A place that does not have four by four handbreadths,
phrases.notes: Located between a public and a private domain.

phrases.english: it is permitted for people of the public domain
and for people of the private domain
to adjust their shoulder loads on it,
provided that they do not exchange objects.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 3's answer by showing that רבי יוחנן applies the same principle elsewhere.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that רבי יוחנן allows people from both sides to use a spot smaller than four by four.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב דימי's report of רבי יוחנן's ruling about a small spot between the public and private domains.

steps.title: Does רב reject רב דימי's ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב, who is strict in the wall case, disagrees with רב דימי's lenient ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does רב not agree with רב דימי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a pointed question about רב. רב forbids even a tiny bit of carrying onto the narrow wall-top, but רב דימי was lenient about a small spot between two domains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רב forbade the people of the two courtyards from lifting even a hair's breadth of food onto the narrow wall-top. רב דימי (Step 4) allowed people from both sides to use a small in-between spot, as long as they do not pass objects to each other. The two rulings seem to clash, so the גמרא asks whether רב really rejects רב דימי.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not hold / does not accept (an opinion)

phrases.english: And does Rav not accept the ruling of Rav Dimi?
phrases.notes: רב's strict ruling on the wall seems to contradict רב דימי's lenient ruling about a small in-between spot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the ruling of רב דימי that was just quoted and asks whether רב's strict position contradicts it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that nothing at all may be lifted onto the narrow wall-top between two courtyards.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב דימי allows people from both sides to use a small in-between spot. If רב forbids all use of the narrow wall-top, he seems to reject a known and accepted ruling.

steps.title: Torah domains versus rabbinic domains
steps.stepSummary: רב agrees with רב דימי for Torah-level domains. The wall case involves rabbinic domains, which חכמים guarded more strictly.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we were talking about domains that exist by Torah law, then yes, רב would agree. But here we are dealing with domains that exist only by rabbinic law, and חכמים made their own laws stronger than Torah laws.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב does accept רב דימי, but only when the two domains are Torah-level domains. The wall between two courtyards is a rabbinic case, and there רב is stricter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב דימי's case is a spot between a public domain and a private domain, and carrying between those is forbidden by Torah law. Carrying between two courtyards without an עירוב is forbidden only by rabbinic law. Because people take rabbinic laws less seriously, חכמים added extra protection to them, so in the courtyard case they forbade even a tiny amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Domains defined by Torah law, like a public domain and a private domain
Domains defined only by rabbinic law, like two courtyards without an עירוב
So too / indeed, that is correct
With what are we dealing here? (introduces a narrower reading of the case)
Reinforcement, extra strengthening

steps.confusionAlert: It sounds backwards that a rabbinic law would be stricter than a Torah law. The idea is that people already treat Torah laws seriously. Rabbinic laws need extra 'fences' so that people do not start treating them lightly.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle, that חכמים reinforced their own rules even more than Torah rules, shows up in many places in ש״ס and explains why some rabbinic laws are surprisingly strict.

phrases.english: If it were about domains by Torah law —
phrases.notes: Such as a public domain and a private domain.

phrases.english: so too (Rav would agree with Rav Dimi).
Here, with what are we dealing?
phrases.notes: Refers to the case of the wall between two courtyards.

phrases.english: With domains by rabbinic law.
phrases.notes: Carrying between two courtyards without an עירוב is only rabbinically forbidden.

phrases.english: And the Sages made reinforcement for their own words
more than for those of the Torah.
phrases.notes: Rabbinic laws need extra protection so people do not treat them lightly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בִּרְשׁוּיוֹת דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא — הָכִי נָמֵי. הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 5 by separating רב דימי's case from רב's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case distinction: Torah-level domains versus rabbinic-level domains.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב rejects רב דימי's leniency entirely.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב accepts רב דימי for Torah-level domains. He is strict only between rabbinic domains, because חכמים reinforced their own laws.

steps.title: A wall high on one side and level on the other
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that a wall which is ten טפחים high on one side and level with the ground on the other belongs to the courtyard on the level side.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said in the name of רב הונא, who said in the name of רב נחמן: a wall between two courtyards that is ten טפחים high on one side and level with the ground on the other side is given to the courtyard where it is level with the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about a wall between two courtyards that is uneven. Only the courtyard on the side where the wall is level with the ground may use the top of the wall on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here one courtyard is lower, so the wall stands a full ten טפחים above it. The other courtyard is higher, so the top of the wall is even with its ground. Instead of letting both courtyards use the wall, the wall is given only to the higher courtyard, whose people can step right onto it.

keyTerms.meaning: A wall
Ten handbreadths, the standard height for a halachic partition
Level with the ground
We give it (its use) to

steps.confusionAlert: 'Level with the ground' does not mean the wall is short. It is the same wall, but the courtyard on that side is built higher up, so the wall's top is even with that courtyard's floor.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה (אָמַר) רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rabba said that Rav Huna said that Rav Naḥman said:
A wall that is between two courtyards,
one side of it is ten handbreadths high
phrases.notes: Facing the lower courtyard.

phrases.english: and its other side is level with the ground —
phrases.notes: Facing the higher courtyard.

phrases.english: we give it to the one where it is level with the ground.
phrases.notes: Only the higher courtyard may use the wall-top on שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה (אָמַר) רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching about walls between courtyards, now dealing with a wall that is uneven on its two sides.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wall that is ten טפחים high on one side and level with the ground on the other belongs only to the courtyard on the level side.

steps.title: Easy use beats hard use
steps.stepSummary: The reason for רב נחמן's ruling: when something is easy for one side to use and hard for the other, it goes to the side with easy use.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because for this side its use is easy, and for that side its use is hard. And whenever something is easy for one and hard for the other, we give it to the one for whom its use is easy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the wall goes to the level courtyard. That side can use it easily, while the other side would have to climb ten טפחים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people of the higher courtyard can simply walk onto the wall-top, but the people of the lower courtyard would struggle to climb up. The גמרא states a general rule for שבת: when one side has easy access and the other has hard access, the space belongs to the easy side. So the lower courtyard loses its right to use the wall.

keyTerms.meaning: Use
Easily, comfortably
With difficulty

steps.whatToRemember: When a wall between two courtyards is easy for one courtyard to use and hard for the other, it is given only to the courtyard with easy access (לזה בנחת ולזה בקשה, נותנין אותו לזה שתשמישו בנחת).
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'לזה בנחת ולזה בקשה, נותנין אותו לזה שתשמישו בנחת' is a general principle for deciding which side controls a shared space in the laws of עירובין.

phrases.english: Because for this one its use is easy
phrases.notes: The higher courtyard steps right onto the wall.

phrases.english: and for that one its use is difficult.
phrases.notes: The lower courtyard must climb ten handbreadths.

phrases.english: And any case where it is easy for this one and difficult for that one —
phrases.notes: A general principle.

phrases.english: we give it to the one whose use is easy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind רב נחמן's ruling in Step 7 and turns it into a general principle.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Shared space goes to the side that can use it easily. A wall level with one courtyard and ten טפחים above the other belongs to the level courtyard.

steps.title: A ditch between two courtyards goes to the side where it is level
steps.stepSummary: רב שיזבי quotes רב נחמן: a ditch that is ten טפחים deep on one side but level with the ground on the other side belongs to the courtyard on the level side.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שיזבי said in the name of רב נחמן: If there is a ditch between two courtyards, and on one side it is ten טפחים deep, but on the other side it is level with the ground, we give the ditch to the courtyard on the level side. The reason is that one side can use it easily and the other side can only use it with difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling from רב נחמן. This one is about a ditch, and it is the mirror image of the wall case we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the wall case, the wall stuck up ten טפחים on one side. Here the ditch goes down ten טפחים on one side. Same logic either way: the side that reaches it easily gets to use it, and the side that would struggle loses its rights.

keyTerms.meaning: A ditch or trench
Ten טפחים deep, the depth that makes it a separate area
Level with the ground, meaning less than ten טפחים deep from that side
We give it, meaning we assign its use to that side

steps.confusionAlert: 'Level with the ground' does not mean the ditch is perfectly flat on that side. It means that from that courtyard the ditch is less than ten טפחים deep, so it is easy to reach.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שֵׁיזְבִי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Sheizvi said that Rav Naḥman said:
A ditch that is between two courtyards,
one side of it is ten handbreadths deep
and its other side is level with the ground —
we give it to the one for whom it is level with the ground,
phrases.notes: Its use is assigned to that courtyard.

phrases.english: because it is a case where
for this one its use is easy
and for that one its use is difficult, etc.
phrases.notes: וכו׳ points back to the rule from step 8: the item goes to the side with easy use.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁיזְבִי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling from רב נחמן that applies the same easy-use principle to a ditch instead of a wall.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ditch ten טפחים deep on one side and level on the other is assigned to the courtyard on the level side, because that side uses it easily.

steps.title: Why the wall case alone would not teach the ditch case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that both rulings are needed. From the wall alone, we might think a ditch is different, because people don't usually use deep places.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both rulings are needed. If רב נחמן had taught us only the wall, we might say the rule works there because people do use high places. But a ditch is different. People do not use deep places, so we might say no one gets to use it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a צריכותא, explaining why רב נחמן had to teach two rulings that look the same. This step covers the first half: why the wall case is not enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Putting things on a high wall is normal and convenient. Bending down into a deep ditch is awkward, so people don't usually use it. We might have thought a ditch is not a usable space at all, so it would not be given to either side.

keyTerms.meaning: And they are both necessary, the opening of a צריכותא
If he had taught us only...
In a high place
In a deep place
I might say not, meaning I would have thought the rule does not apply

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody actually asked 'why do we need both?' out loud. The word וּצְרִיכִי answers that unspoken question by itself.

phrases.english: And they are both necessary.
For if he had taught us only the wall,
I would say it is because people do use a high place.
But a ditch,
people do not use a deep place —
I might say the rule does not apply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the unspoken question of why רב נחמן needed to teach the ditch ruling right after the wall ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: shows each case has a different reason to doubt it, so neither teaches the other
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A ditch might not be usable at all, since people don't put things in deep places, so neither side would get it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ditch ruling had to be said on its own, because the wall ruling would not have covered it.

steps.title: Why the ditch case alone would not teach the wall case
steps.stepSummary: From the ditch alone, we might think a wall is different, because things placed on a wall may fall. So both rulings are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he had taught us only the ditch, we might say the rule works there because using it is not risky. But a wall is risky to use, so we might say no one gets to use it. That is why both rulings are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the צריכותא with the second half: the ditch case would not have taught us the wall case. It then concludes that both rulings are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something placed in a ditch is safe and will not fall. Something placed on top of a wall can fall off, so people worry about using it. Each case has its own weakness, so רב נחמן had to say both.

keyTerms.meaning: Worrisome, causing fear
Its use
It is necessary, the closing word of a צריכותא

steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן's two rulings, the wall and the ditch, share one principle: the side with easy use gets the space. Each ruling still had to be taught on its own. The wall is convenient but risky. The ditch is safe but awkward.

phrases.english: And if he had taught us only about a ditch,
I would say it is because its use is not worrisome.
But a wall, whose use is worrisome —
phrases.notes: Objects may fall off it.

phrases.english: I might say the rule does not apply,
therefore both are necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכותא begun in step 10 by showing the opposite direction, then concludes.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both the wall ruling and the ditch ruling are needed, because each case has a different reason we might have thought the rule does not apply.

steps.title: Lowering part of a wall: four handbreadths makes the whole wall usable
steps.stepSummary: If someone lowers part of a tall wall and the lowered section is four טפחים wide, the whole wall may be used. If it is less, only the part across from the lowered section may be used.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone comes to lower the height of the wall, and the lowered section is four טפחים wide, he may use the entire wall. If it is not four טפחים wide, he may use only the part of the wall across from the lowered section.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new rule about the wall between two courtyards. It explains what happens if someone lowers part of it to below ten טפחים, for example by putting a stone or platform next to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lowered section four טפחים wide counts as a real usable opening, so it changes the status of the whole wall and all of it may be used. A smaller section is too narrow to count. It only helps for the small spot right across from it, and the rest of the wall stays forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He comes to reduce it, meaning to lower the wall's effective height
Its reduced section
Four טפחים, the minimum size for a significant area
Opposite the reduced section only

steps.confusionAlert: 'Four' here is about how WIDE the lowered section is, not how much the height was lowered. The height must already be brought below ten טפחים. The four טפחים decides whether the change affects the whole wall.
steps.whyThisMatters: This uses the familiar size of four טפחים. A space that size counts as significant and can change the status of everything around it. A smaller space only matters for itself.

phrases.english: If he comes to diminish it,
phrases.notes: For example by placing a stone or platform next to the wall.

phrases.english: if its diminished section is four handbreadths wide —
it is permitted to use the entire wall, all of it.
And if not —
he may use only the area opposite the diminished section.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the צריכותא ends, the גמרא opens a new topic about the wall: changing its height to make it usable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the lowered section of a wall is four טפחים wide, the whole wall may be used. If not, only the area opposite the lowered section may be used.

steps.title: Challenge: the narrow lowered section should help either fully or not at all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the ruling from Step 12. Either the lowering works, so the whole wall may be used, or it does not work, so even the lowered spot should be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it, this is hard. If the lowering is effective, let him use the whole wall. If it is not effective, then even the part across from the lowered section should not be allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling it just quoted about a lowered section that is less than four טפחים wide.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling in Step 12 took a middle position: only the part across from the lowered section may be used. The גמרא argues there is no logical middle. Either the narrow lowering counts and changes the status of the wall, or it is too small to matter at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you look at it. This introduces a two-sided challenge.
It was effective, it worked
The lowering, the reducing of the wall's height
Across from, opposite

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is about to lay out two possibilities, and either way leads to a problem.

phrases.english: If the lowering is effective —
let him use the entire wall.
If it is not effective —
then even the part across from the lowered section should also not be allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the internal logic of the ruling in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a lowered section less than four טפחים wide allows use only of the part across from it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is a dilemma. A lowering either counts or it does not, so a partial result makes no sense.

steps.title: רבינא: a stone was actually removed from the top of the wall
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains that the case is one where a piece was physically removed from the top of the wall. That spot is truly low, but it is too narrow to change the status of the whole wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The case is where he removed a stone segment from the top of the wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge by explaining what kind of lowering the ruling is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the wall really is shorter at that spot, because nothing was added and part of the wall was taken away. So that narrow spot is usable on its own, like an opening in the wall. Since it is less than four טפחים wide, though, it does not change the status of the whole wall. This explains the middle ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: He uprooted or removed
A segment or layer, such as a row of stone
From its top

steps.whatToRemember: A narrow spot that is physically lowered is usable by itself, but it does not make the whole wall usable unless it is four טפחים wide.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
For example, where he removed a segment from its top.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: כְּגוֹן שֶׁעָקַר חוּלְיָא מֵרֹאשׁוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the dilemma raised in Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the ruling is set in a specific physical situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed the lowering either counts for the whole wall or not at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: A piece was actually removed from the wall. That narrow spot is truly low and usable, but it is too small to change the rest of the wall.

steps.title: רב יחיאל: an upside-down basin lowers the wall
steps.stepSummary: רב יחיאל rules that if someone turns a basin upside down next to the wall, it counts as reducing the wall's height.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יחיאל said: If one turned a basin upside down next to the wall, it reduces the wall's height.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ruling is brought: something placed next to a wall, such as an overturned basin, can make the wall count as shorter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the lowering was done by taking something away from the top of the wall. רב יחיאל adds a different method: raising the ground next to the wall by placing an object there. This makes the wall less than ten טפחים high when measured from the top of the basin.

keyTerms.meaning: He turned upside down
A basin or bowl
It reduces, it lowers the effective height

phrases.english: Rav Yeḥiel said:
If one turned over a basin, it reduces the height.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְחִיאֵל: כָּפָה סֵפֶל מְמַעֵט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling on a related subject: lowering a wall by adding something next to it, instead of removing something from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An upside-down basin placed by a wall counts as reducing the wall's height.

steps.title: Challenge: a basin can be moved on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the basin should count, since it can be moved on שבת. An object that may be moved on שבת does not lower a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why should that be? It is an object that may be moved on שבת, and an object that may be moved on שבת does not reduce the wall's height.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יחיאל's ruling using a known principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something that can be picked up and taken away at any moment on שבת is not a permanent part of the wall area. Since a basin is a regular utensil that may be moved, it should not change the wall's height.

keyTerms.meaning: And why? This opens a challenge.
An object that may be moved on שבת

steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not that the basin is too small. The problem is that it is not permanent, because it may be moved away on שבת.

phrases.english: And why?
It is an item that may be moved on Shabbat,
and an item that may be moved on Shabbat does not reduce the height.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יחיאל's ruling in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יחיאל's ruling that an overturned basin reduces the wall's height.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A known principle says that movable objects do not lower a wall, and a basin is movable on שבת.

steps.title: Answer: the basin was attached to the ground
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is where the basin was attached to the ground by covering it with earth, so it may not be moved on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where he attached it to the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב יחיאל by narrowing his ruling to a basin that was fixed into the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once earth covers the basin, moving it would mean moving the earth, which is מוקצה. So the basin is no longer something that may be moved on שבת, and it can count as a permanent reduction of the wall's height.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for a case where. This narrows a ruling to a specific case.
He attached it to the ground

phrases.english: No, it is necessary,
where he attached it to the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to an attached basin.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A basin is a movable utensil, so it cannot lower the wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The basin was covered with earth, so it may not be moved on שבת and it does count.

steps.title: Challenge: attaching to the ground may not stop it from being moved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what difference attaching to the ground makes. A ברייתא teaches that a fig buried in straw or a cake buried in coals may still be taken out on שבת if part of it is showing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he attached it to the ground, so what? Wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: an unripe fig that one buried in straw, or a cake that one buried in coals, if part of it is uncovered, it may be taken on שבת?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 17 by bringing a ברייתא. The next step answers this challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows that an object partly covered by מוקצה material, such as straw or coals, may still be pulled out on שבת, as long as part of it is showing. In the same way, a basin covered with earth would still be movable, so it should not lower the wall. Step 19 answers this challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: What of it? So what difference does it make?
But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא? This introduces a source used to challenge.
An unripe fig
A flat cake baked on coals
He buried or covered it
Part of it is uncovered or visible

phrases.english: And if he attached it to the ground, what of it?
But wasn't it taught in a baraita:
An unripe fig that one buried in straw,
and a cake that one buried in coals,
if part of it is uncovered —
it may be taken on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי חַבְּרֵיהּ בְּאַרְעָא, מַאי הָוֵי? וְהָא תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a basin attached to the ground with earth may not be moved on שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא permits taking out food that is partly buried in מוקצה material, so a partly covered basin would also be movable and would not lower the wall.

steps.title: The basin has a buried rim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the basin has a rim sunk into the earth, so lifting it out would dig up the ground. That makes it forbidden to move on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the basin has a rim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 18. It says this basin is different from the fig or cake because it has a rim buried in the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, a fig or cake could be pulled out without really disturbing the straw or coals. Here the basin's rim is stuck deep in the earth, so pulling it out breaks up the ground, which is like digging on שבת. Since it may not be moved, the basin is fixed in place, and רב יחיאל's ruling can stand.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? This phrase introduces a narrower case to answer a question.
Rims or edges of a vessel

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
Where it has rims.
phrases.notes: The rim is buried in the earth, so removing the basin would dig up soil.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 18 from the fig-and-cake ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): the basin has a buried rim.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Covering the basin with earth alone does not fix it in place, because buried items may still be pulled out on שבת.
steps.terutzMaskana: A basin whose rim is sunk in the ground cannot be pulled out without digging, so it is fixed in place and lowers the wall.

steps.title: Challenge from a buried turnip or radish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what difference a buried rim makes. It begins quoting a משנה about someone who buries a turnip or radish under a vine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it has rims, what of it? Didn't we learn in a משנה: One who buries a turnip or a radish under a vine, when...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 19. It starts quoting a משנה to show that something stuck in the ground may still be pulled out on שבת. The quote continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A turnip or radish buried in the earth is also held tightly by the soil, like a basin with a rim. The משנה will teach that, in certain conditions, it may still be taken out on שבת. If so, the basin's rim should not make it forbidden to move either.

keyTerms.meaning: What of it? What difference does it make?
One who buries or hides something
A turnip and a radish
A grapevine

steps.confusionAlert: The quote is cut off at the word בִּזְמַן ('when'). The condition and the ruling of the משנה come on the next amud, so do not decide the answer yet.

phrases.english: And if it has rims,
what of it? But didn't we learn in a mishna:
One who buries a turnip or a radish
beneath a vine, when...
phrases.notes: The quote continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי אִית לֵיהּ אוֹגְנַיִים, מַאי הָוֵי? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the buried-rim answer from Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 19 that a buried rim makes the basin forbidden to move on שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה about a turnip or radish buried under a vine will suggest that pulling an item out of the ground on שבת is allowed even though the soil holds it tightly. So the rim should make no difference.
